System design · Module 07 of 29 · Level 2: Building blocks

API design: contracts that are safe to call, retry and change

An API is a promise to everyone who calls it. Once apps depend on it, it's hard to change, so the decisions you make on day one last for years. This module covers how to shape resources and errors, page through long lists without losing items, make retries safe, evolve without breaking clients, and when gRPC or GraphQL fit better than REST.

1. The idea

A restaurant menu is an API. It names the dishes (resources), says what you can do (order, change, cancel), and what you'll get back. A good menu is consistent ("all mains come with a side"), never changes a dish's meaning without warning, and a good waiter, asked twice for the same order because you weren't sure they heard, brings one meal, not two.

Most public and product APIs are REST: you act on resources (nouns) using a small set of HTTP methods (verbs).

MethodMeaningExampleSafe to repeat?
GETRead; never changes anythingGET /events/42Yes
POSTCreate (server picks the ID), or start an actionPOST /events/42/bookingsNo, unless you add an idempotency key
PUTReplace the whole resourcePUT /users/7/avatarYes
PATCHChange some fieldsPATCH /bookings/9 {"seats": 3}Depends on the change
DELETERemoveDELETE /bookings/9Yes

"Safe to repeat" is idempotency: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. It matters because networks fail after the server acted but before the client heard back, so clients retry, and a non-idempotent retry can charge a card twice.

Shaping the request

  • Path identifies the resource: /events/42/tickets. Use plural nouns and nesting for ownership; never verbs (/getTickets).
  • Query parameters are optional filters, sorting and paging: ?section=VIP&sort=-price&limit=20.
  • Body carries the data being created or changed.
  • Headers carry metadata: Authorization, Idempotency-Key, If-Match, caching headers.
  • Identity comes from the token, never from a userId in the body. The server then checks the caller may touch this resource (authorization).

2. How it works

Paging through a list that keeps changing

Every list that grows (posts, orders, messages) needs pagination. There are two common ways. Press Play to see what happens when new posts arrive while a user scrolls.

-- Offset: simple, lets users jump to page 7, but drifts and gets slow deep down (the DB still walks the skipped rows)
SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;

-- Cursor (keyset): stable under inserts, fast at any depth with an index on (created_at, id)
SELECT * FROM posts WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

Return the cursor as an opaque string ("next": "eyJ0IjoiMjAyNi0x...") so you can change what's inside it later. Always cap limit.

Errors that clients can act on

Use the right status class (4xx: the caller must change something; 5xx: our fault, maybe retry) and one error shape everywhere. RFC 9457 ("Problem Details") standardises it:

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "https://api.example.com/errors/seat-taken",
 "title": "Seat no longer available",
 "status": 409,
 "detail": "Seat 14C was booked by someone else.",
 "instance": "/events/42/bookings"}

Making POST safe to retry

The client generates a unique idempotency key (a random UUID) per logical operation and sends it with every attempt. The server stores the key with the result; a repeat of the same key returns the stored result instead of acting again. Stripe popularised this (keys up to 255 characters, kept for at least 24 hours), and the IETF is standardising the Idempotency-Key header (still a draft in October 2026). Try it in section 3.

Long-running work: 202 and a job

If a request starts something slow (a video encode, a report), don't hold the connection open. Return 202 Accepted with a job resource, Location: /jobs/123, and let the client poll it, or call the client back with a webhook when it's done. Sign webhooks (an HMAC of the body with a shared secret) so receivers can verify they came from you, and expect them to arrive more than once.

Changing an API without breaking clients

  • Safe changes: adding endpoints, adding optional fields, adding new values clients are told to ignore.
  • Breaking changes: renaming or removing fields, changing types or meanings, making optional input required.
  • Versioning: breaking changes go in a new version, usually in the path (/v2/), sometimes in a header or a dated version (Stripe-Version: 2026-09-30). Keep the old version running with a published end date.

3. Try it yourself

Retry a payment over a flaky network

Each click sends POST /payments {"amount": 50}. With "lose the response" on, the server charges the card but the reply never reaches the app, so the app retries. Try it with and without an idempotency key.

Spot the API smells

4. REST, gRPC or GraphQL?

REST (JSON over HTTP)gRPC (Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2)GraphQL
Best forPublic APIs, web and mobile clients, most product APIsService-to-service calls inside your systemMany different clients needing different slices of rich, connected data
StrengthsSimple, universal, cacheable by CDNs and browsers, easy to debug with curlCompact binary messages, typed contracts and generated clients in many languages, streaming, deadlinesClient asks for exactly the fields it needs in one request; one schema for many teams
WeaknessesOver- or under-fetching; many round trips for nested data; schema is optional (use OpenAPI)Not usable directly from browsers (needs gRPC-Web or a gateway); harder to inspect by handHard to cache at the HTTP layer; the N+1 query problem (fix with batching "dataloaders"); per-field authorization; expensive queries need limits
Interview defaultYes, for anything user-facingMention for internal calls when performance mattersOnly when the prompt stresses varied clients or rapid front-end change

Real-time push (WebSockets, server-sent events) is a different problem: Module 19.

5. In real systems

  • Describe the API in a schema: OpenAPI (version 3.2 in October 2026) for REST, .proto files for gRPC, an SDL schema for GraphQL. Generate docs, client libraries and request validation from it, and review changes to it like code.
  • Put cross-cutting rules in a gateway: an API gateway (Module 08) handles authentication, rate limits (returning 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After), request size limits and logging, so each service doesn't reimplement them.
  • Auth: end users usually present a short-lived signed token (a JWT from an OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect login), verified without a database call; services use their own credentials (Module 26). API keys suit server-to-server integrations, not end users.
  • Deadlines and timeouts: gRPC lets callers set a deadline that travels with the request through every downstream call, so work stops when the caller has given up.
  • Optimistic concurrency over HTTP: GET returns an ETag; the client sends If-Match: "v7" on its PUT; the server answers 412 Precondition Failed if someone changed it meanwhile (Module 17).
  • Style guides worth borrowing: Google's API design guide, Microsoft's REST guidelines and Zalando's RESTful guidelines.

In an interview, spend about five minutes here: list the endpoints for the core requirements with their main inputs and outputs, mention pagination on any list and an idempotency key on any payment or booking, and move on.

6. Remember it

Memory hook: "Nouns, verbs, and a receipt"Resources are nouns, methods are verbs, and every important write carries a receipt number (an idempotency key) so asking twice can't buy twice.
How this hook works: what "Nouns, verbs, and a receipt" means

What the slogan means, phrase by phrase

"Nouns"
Resources in the path, plural and nested by ownership: /users/7/bookings, not /getUserBookings.
"verbs"
The HTTP methods, with their standard meanings: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes, DELETE removes.
"a receipt"
An idempotency key on non-idempotent writes, so retries are safe. The receipt idea extends to cursors (a bookmark into a list) and ETags (a version stamp).

Why this picture fits: a shop counter works the same way: you name the item, say what you want done, and keep a receipt so a dispute or a repeat doesn't charge you twice.

The story → the concept

At the counterIn the API
The item on the shelfA resource and its URL
"I'd like to buy / return / swap"POST / DELETE / PUT or PATCH
The receipt numberThe idempotency key
"Show me the next ten after this one"A pagination cursor
The price tag's dateAn ETag version for safe updates
The shop's printed rulesThe OpenAPI schema and error format

Watch it on an example

Designing a ticket booking API:

  1. Nouns: /events, /events/{id}/seats, /bookings.
  2. Verbs: GET /events?city=Pune&cursor=…, POST /bookings, DELETE /bookings/{id}.
  3. Receipt: POST /bookings requires an Idempotency-Key, so a double-tap or a retry books once.
  4. The user comes from the token; the server checks the booking belongs to them before a DELETE.

The trap it saves you from

Action-shaped endpoints (/bookTicketForUser?id=7) and retry bugs that double-charge, both of which are painful to fix once clients depend on them.

It still works when…

You're designing messages for a queue (Module 18). Name the event as a noun-plus-past-tense ("BookingCreated"), and give it an ID consumers can use to ignore duplicates: the same receipt idea.

7. Common mistakes

Trusting a user ID in the requestDELETE /bookings/9?userId=7 lets anyone delete anyone's booking. Identify the caller from the token, and check ownership.
Unbounded listsAn endpoint that returns "all orders" works in testing and times out in production. Paginate every list and cap the page size.
Errors inside a 200200 OK {"error": "not found"} breaks every client library, cache and monitor. Use the right status code.
Retrying non-idempotent writes blindlyRetries without an idempotency key turn a network blip into duplicate orders.
Breaking changes without a versionRenaming a field breaks old app versions that users haven't updated. Add, don't change; version when you must.

8. Design exercise (25 minutes)

  1. Design the API for a food delivery app: browse restaurants near me, view a menu, place an order, track the order. Write each endpoint with method, path, key inputs and response.
  2. Make it safe: which endpoints need an idempotency key? Which lists need pagination, and offset or cursor?
  3. Errors: write the response for "restaurant closed" and for "payment declined". Which status codes?
  4. Evolve it: the product now wants scheduled orders. Add it without breaking existing clients.
  5. Write it down: your three favourite rules from this page in your design notebook.

9. Self-check quiz

Which is the most RESTful way to list a user's orders?

A plural noun nested under its owner, read with GET. (The server still checks the caller may see user 7's orders.)

An infinite-scroll feed gets new posts every second. Which pagination keeps items from repeating?

A cursor remembers where you stopped, so inserts at the top don't shift what "the next page" means.

A client retries POST /payments with the same idempotency key. What should happen?

That's the whole point of the key: the server recognises the repeat and replays the stored result.

Two internal services exchange thousands of small typed messages per second. Which fits best?

Compact binary encoding, generated typed clients, HTTP/2 multiplexing and deadlines make gRPC the usual internal choice.
